title: A HUSBAND’S BED BECAME PART OF A BARGAIN BETWEEN TWO RIVAL SISTERS—AND GOD SAW THE PAIN NEITHER WOMAN COULD HIDE
paragraphs: A HUSBAND’S BED BECAME PART OF A BARGAIN BETWEEN TWO RIVAL SISTERS—AND GOD SAW THE PAIN NEITHER WOMAN COULD HIDE

Two sisters. One husband. A handful of mandrakes. One desperate bargain. But beneath one of the Bible’s strangest family scandals lies a devastating truth about jealousy, rejection, the hunger to be loved, and the God who refuses to abandon broken people.

“And Leah said, A little thing is it that thou hast taken my husband? and wouldest thou take away my son's mandrakes also? And Rachel said, Therefore he shall lie with thee to night for thy son's mandrakes.” — Genesis 30:15, KJV
Imagine being married to a man who comes home to you…
But whose heart belongs to someone else.
Imagine sharing his name, bearing his children, managing his household, and waking up every morning knowing that if he could choose all over again, he would choose your sister.
Now imagine being that sister.
The one he loves.
The one he worked seven years to marry.
The one everyone assumes must be happy because she possesses the affection the other woman desperately wants.
Except every time you hear a baby cry in the next room, something inside you breaks.
Because the child belongs to her.
And your arms are empty.
One woman had children but longed to be loved.
The other was loved but longed to have children.
And one evening, in a household already poisoned by comparison, a few plants gathered from a field became the price of a night in their husband’s bed.
Yes. That actually happened in the Bible.
But before you shake your head at these women, you may want to look carefully at what drove them there.
Because their story is not merely about an ancient family behaving scandalously.
It is about what happens when wounded people begin bargaining for things they were never meant to purchase.
Love.
Worth.
Acceptance.
Security.
The assurance that they matter.
And somewhere inside this uncomfortable story, you may recognize a version of yourself.
Not because you have ever traded mandrakes.
But because perhaps you, too, have spent years trying to earn what your heart desperately needed someone to give freely.
The story begins long before the strange exchange recorded in Genesis 30.
Jacob loved Rachel.
Genesis 29:18 tells us plainly, “And Jacob loved Rachel.”
He agreed to serve her father, Laban, for seven years in order to marry her. Scripture says those years seemed to him like only a few days because of his love for her.
It sounds like the beginning of a beautiful romance.
Until the wedding night.
Laban deceived Jacob and gave him Leah, Rachel’s older sister, instead. When morning came, Jacob discovered the deception.
The deceiver had been deceived.
Jacob, who had previously deceived his own father in the matter of the blessing, now experienced betrayal within his own family.
But Leah was not merely a detail in someone else’s lesson.
She was a woman.
A daughter.
A sister.
A wife whose marriage began under circumstances she had not been shown freely choosing.
And the morning Jacob discovered that the woman beside him was not Rachel, Leah entered a marriage already overshadowed by another woman's place in his heart.
Jacob eventually married Rachel as well, agreeing to additional years of service.
Then Scripture delivers a sentence that reveals the emotional tragedy inside that household.
“And he loved also Rachel more than Leah.” — Genesis 29:30, KJV
More than Leah.
Those three words carry a lifetime of sorrow.
Leah did not have to wonder whether her husband preferred her sister.
Scripture tells us he did.
And God saw it.
Genesis 29:31 says:
“And when the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren.”
The Hebrew word translated “hated” is שְׂנוּאָה (senu'ah), from the root שׂנא (sana').

In this context, the language describes Leah’s painful position as the less-loved wife. It does not require us to conclude that Jacob expressed active hostility toward her every day. Genesis 29:30 explicitly establishes the comparison: Rachel was loved more.
That distinction matters.
Because sometimes the deepest wounds do not come from someone openly declaring hatred.
Sometimes they come from being tolerated when you ache to be cherished.
Being included but never preferred.
Being present but feeling invisible.
And if you have ever lived in the shadow of someone else's affection, you understand why those words hurt.
God saw Leah.
Notice what the text does not say.
It does not say Leah became valuable when she gave Jacob children.
It does not say she earned God’s attention by becoming useful.
It says the LORD saw her condition.
Before the rivalry reached its strangest moment, God was already aware of the wounded woman inside the marriage.
Leah conceived and gave birth to Reuben.
She said, “Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me.” — Genesis 29:32, KJV
There it is.
The hope underneath the childbirth.
Now he will love me.
Not simply, “I have a son.”
Not merely, “My family is growing.”
But perhaps now, after giving him something precious, she would finally become precious to him.
Then Simeon was born.
Leah said the LORD had heard that she was hated.
Then Levi.
And her words revealed the same aching hope:
“Now this time will my husband be joined unto me.” — Genesis 29:34, KJV
Can you hear her?
Perhaps this child will change everything.
Perhaps now he will stay.
Perhaps now he will look at me the way he looks at Rachel.
Perhaps now I will be enough.
But a child cannot heal every wound in a marriage.
And no human being, not even a beloved son or daughter, should be forced to carry the burden of proving that a parent deserves love.
Then Leah gave birth to Judah.
This time, her recorded words changed.
“Now will I praise the LORD.” — Genesis 29:35, KJV
The name Judah is associated with praise, from the Hebrew root ידה (yadah), meaning to praise or give thanks.
For a moment, the focus of Leah’s words moves from her husband’s affection to the LORD.
It is a beautiful moment.
But Scripture does not pretend that one declaration of praise instantly erased every insecurity Leah had ever carried.
Her story continued.
Her wounds were real.
And soon, the rivalry intensified.
Rachel, meanwhile, was suffering in a different way.
Genesis 30:1 records her anguish:
“Give me children, or else I die.”
She spoke those words to Jacob.
The woman who had his love was overwhelmed by what she did not have.
And Jacob became angry.
“Am I in God's stead, who hath withheld from thee the fruit of the womb?” — Genesis 30:2, KJV
Jacob could not give Rachel the thing she demanded.
And his angry response did not heal her grief.
So Rachel gave her servant Bilhah to Jacob, and children were born through that arrangement. Leah later gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob as well.
The women were not merely competing emotionally anymore.
Their rivalry had drawn other people into the struggle.
Bilhah and Zilpah were servants living in a deeply unequal household. Scripture records their involvement without inviting us to romanticize the lack of power they had in these arrangements.
This was a family marked by deception, favoritism, polygamy, competition, and wounded relationships.
The Bible reports these realities.
It does not command believers to reproduce them.
And then came the mandrakes.
Genesis 30:14 tells us that Reuben, Leah’s son, went into the field during wheat harvest and found mandrakes.
The Hebrew word is דּוּדָאִים (duda'im).
Mandrakes were plants associated in the ancient world with love and fertility. Their appearance in the story is especially significant because Rachel was struggling with infertility.
But the biblical text never teaches that mandrakes can overcome infertility, nor does it attribute Rachel’s eventual conception to their power.
That distinction is crucial.
Rachel saw what Reuben had brought to Leah.
And she wanted some.
“Give me, I pray thee, of thy son's mandrakes.” — Genesis 30:14, KJV
It sounds like a small request.
A few plants.
Something gathered from a field.
But Leah’s response exposed the wound that had been festering beneath the surface.
“Is it a small matter that thou hast taken my husband? and wouldest thou take away my son's mandrakes also?” — Genesis 30:15, KJV, with modernized punctuation
Stop there.
Read that again.
“Thou hast taken my husband.”
Leah was speaking to the woman Jacob loved more.
Rachel was not a stranger.
She was her sister.
They had grown up in the same family.
And now the relationship that should have offered companionship had become a source of bitterness.
Leah saw Rachel as someone who had taken the affection she longed for.
Rachel saw Leah living the motherhood she desperately desired.
Both women looked across the same household and saw something they believed would finally make them whole.
And neither seemed able to enjoy what she possessed without being tormented by what the other had.
Isn't that what comparison does?
It convinces you that your life cannot be meaningful while someone else possesses something you lack.
You see another person's marriage and question your own worth.
You see someone else's children and quietly grieve the family you hoped to have.
You see another person's success, ministry, beauty, opportunities, or relationships, and suddenly your blessings feel smaller.
You may genuinely love God.
You may sincerely rejoice with others.
And still find yourself asking in the privacy of your heart:
Lord, why them and not me?
That question does not always come from arrogance.
Sometimes it comes from grief.
Sometimes it comes from waiting.
Sometimes it comes from the exhaustion of watching another person receive what you have prayed for through years of tears.
But if grief is allowed to become resentment, it can turn another person's blessing into an accusation against God.
Rachel wanted the mandrakes.
Leah wanted time with Jacob.
And Rachel made an offer.
“Therefore he shall lie with thee to night for thy son's mandrakes.” — Genesis 30:15, KJV
There it was.
A bargain.
Rachel offered Leah a night with their husband in exchange for the plants.
Genesis 30:16 records what happened when Jacob returned from the field.
“And Leah went out to meet him, and said, Thou must come in unto me; for surely I have hired thee with my son's mandrakes.”
The Hebrew expression behind “I have hired thee” is שָׂכֹר שְׂכַרְתִּיךָ (sakhor sekhartikha), an emphatic construction from the root שׂכר (sakhar), associated with hiring or wages.
The language is startling.
Leah spoke as though she had secured Jacob’s company through a transaction.
And the verse ends:
“And he lay with her that night.”
No romantic speech.
No tender reconciliation recorded.
No evidence that Jacob suddenly loved Leah as she had always hoped.
Only the painful fact that a night with her husband had become something negotiated between sisters.
The text does not tell us everything Jacob thought or felt that evening, and we should not invent details Scripture does not reveal.
But what Scripture does reveal is heartbreaking enough.
A wife had come to speak of her husband’s companionship in the language of hiring.
And another wife had treated access to that companionship as something she could exchange.
A relationship had become a transaction.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story reaches into the modern world with uncomfortable precision.
Because many people are still bargaining for affection.
They just use different currencies.
Some bargain with money.
Some with physical intimacy.
Some with constant agreement.
Some with silence.
Some with relentless achievement.
Some with service so exhausting that they no longer know who they are apart from what they do for others.
They keep giving because they are afraid that if they stop being useful, they will stop being wanted.
They keep apologizing even when they have done nothing wrong because peace feels safer than honesty.
They keep hiding their pain because they believe being difficult to love is the same as being unworthy of love.
And some carry that same pattern into their relationship with God.
They begin treating prayer like payment.
Obedience like a negotiation.
Generosity like a way to purchase divine attention.
Religious activity like evidence that God now owes them an answer.
Lord, I have served You. Why am I still waiting?
Lord, I have given so much. Why does my family still hurt?
Lord, I have tried to do everything right. Why do I still feel forgotten?
But the living God is not a merchant selling His mercy to the highest bidder.
And His grace is not merchandise that can be purchased through spiritual performance.
Listen carefully to what happens next in Genesis.
After the exchange, Leah conceived again.
Genesis 30:17 says:
“And God hearkened unto Leah, and she conceived, and bare Jacob the fifth son.”
The Hebrew wording begins וַיִּשְׁמַע אֱלֹהִים אֶל־לֵאָה (vayyishma Elohim el-Le'ah), meaning that God listened to Leah.
The text does not say the mandrakes caused the conception.
It does not say the bargain compelled God to act.
It says God listened.
Later, Leah named her son Issachar, connecting his birth to the language of wages or reward in Genesis 30:18.
Her interpretation of events reflected her own understanding of her circumstances. The narrator, however, had already directed the reader to God's action.
This is one of the most important distinctions in the entire account.
The people in the story were trying to manage their lives through competition, arrangements, and bargaining.
But the narrator kept directing attention to God.
And then, after further developments, the story turns toward Rachel.
Genesis 30:22 says:
“And God remembered Rachel, and God hearkened to her, and opened her womb.”
The Hebrew begins וַיִּזְכֹּר אֱלֹהִים אֶת־רָחֵל (vayyizkor Elohim et-Rachel).
“And God remembered Rachel.”
In biblical language, God remembering someone does not mean He had previously forgotten that person existed.
It often signals His attentive action on their behalf.
The same God who saw Leah's affliction now acted for Rachel.
Not because Rachel had found the perfect plant.
Not because she had outmaneuvered her sister.
Not because she had finally discovered a technique that forced heaven to cooperate.
God remembered Rachel.
And Joseph was born.
The two sisters had spent years competing for what the other possessed.
Yet neither woman was outside God's sight.
Now be careful here.
This does not mean every person struggling with infertility will eventually conceive.
It does not mean every wounded marriage will be restored.
It does not mean every painful wait ends with the exact outcome we desire.
Genesis tells us what God did in this particular family. It does not give us permission to promise every reader the same earthly result.
Some prayers are answered differently than we hoped.
Some losses remain painful.
Some relationships require boundaries, repentance, counseling, or separation for safety rather than another attempt to purchase affection.
And some faithful believers carry grief that will not be fully healed in this present life.
But the gospel gives us something deeper than a guarantee that every circumstance will change.
It gives us the assurance that our acceptance before God does not depend on possessing the life we imagined.
And this is where the story becomes more astonishing than the scandal itself.
Because the family did not end with mandrakes.
The story continued through generations.
And one name rises from Leah’s children with extraordinary significance.
Judah.
The son whose name was associated with praise.
The son born to the woman who knew what it felt like to be less loved.
The son through whose family line the biblical story would eventually lead toward the Messiah.
Genesis 49:10 connects royal expectation with Judah.
Matthew 1 traces Jesus Christ's royal genealogy through Judah.
Hebrews 7:14 declares:
“For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda.”
And Revelation 5:5 calls Jesus “the Lion of the tribe of Juda.”
Do you see the astonishing movement of Scripture?
Leah was not the wife Jacob loved most.
Yet God chose the line of Judah, her son, as the royal line through which the promised Messiah would come.
That does not mean Leah earned this privilege through suffering.
It does not mean her painful marriage was good.
And it certainly does not mean God approves of deception or marital rivalry because He can accomplish His purposes amid them.
It means human brokenness did not overthrow God's redemptive purpose.
The household was fractured.
The relationships were wounded.
The choices were often deeply flawed.
But God was not defeated by the disorder.
And generations later, Jesus Christ entered the world.
Not to endorse the sins of His ancestors.
Not to glorify their dysfunction.
But to save sinners.
Including the jealous.
The rejected.
The deceptive.
The bitter.
The sexually broken.
The spiritually exhausted.
The people who have harmed others.
And the people who have been harmed.
The people who have tried to earn love because they never believed they could simply receive it.
John 1:14 says:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.”
Grace and truth.
Not grace without truth, pretending sin is harmless.
Not truth without grace, crushing every wounded soul beneath condemnation.
Jesus came full of both.
He does not call bitterness righteousness merely because it began in pain.
He does not excuse manipulation because someone feels rejected.
He does not bless jealousy because longing is understandable.
He exposes what is wrong.
And He invites sinners to come to Him for mercy.
At the cross, we encounter something radically different from Leah and Rachel's bargain.
Leah tried to secure a night of companionship through an exchange.
Rachel tried to obtain what she believed might help her conceive.
Both were reaching for something they could not ultimately control.
But Jesus Christ did not come offering a transaction by which sinners could purchase salvation.
He came to give Himself.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
A gift.
Not wages.
Not a negotiated reward.
Not a divine favor purchased by impressive religious performance.
A gift.
And that gift was costly.
Not to the sinner who receives it by faith, but to the Savior who gave His life.
First Peter 2:24 says Christ “his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree.”
The One who never sinned bore the sins of others.
The One worthy of all honor endured shame.
The One who owed us nothing gave Himself for our redemption.
And the risen Christ now calls people everywhere to repent and believe the gospel.
Maybe you have spent your life feeling like Leah.
You have done everything you know to do.
You have given.
You have served.
You have endured.
You have tried to become indispensable.
And somewhere inside, a wounded voice still whispers:
Maybe this time I will finally be loved.
Or maybe you understand Rachel.
People look at your life and assume you have everything.
They see what is visible.
They compliment what is beautiful.
They envy what appears successful.
But they do not see the private ache.
The unanswered prayer.
The empty space at the table.
The diagnosis.
The marriage that never happened.
The child you never held.
The family you hoped would reconcile.
The dream that slowly became too painful to mention.
And you have wondered whether God notices the part of your life nobody else can see.
The answer of Scripture is not that your pain is imaginary.
Nor is it that you should be ashamed for grieving.
The answer is that Jesus Christ meets sinners and sufferers with truth, compassion, and a call to trust Him.
He sees what others overlook.
He knows what others misunderstand.
And He is able to save completely those who come to God through Him (Hebrews 7:25).
Perhaps the hardest thing for you to surrender is not your sin alone.
Perhaps it is the belief that once you obtain the thing you desperately want, you will finally become whole.
Once they apologize.
Once they choose you.
Once the money arrives.
Once the child is born.
Once the relationship begins.
Once the promotion comes.
Once the people who rejected you finally acknowledge your worth.
Then, you tell yourself, you will have peace.
But what happens if that day never comes?
Will you still have a reason to live?
Will you still have a reason to worship?
Will you still believe Christ is worthy?
The gospel does not ask us to pretend that earthly desires do not matter.
Marriage matters.
Children matter.
Belonging matters.
Justice matters.
Healing matters.
But none of these things can bear the full weight of being our savior.
Only Jesus can.
And the deepest scandal of Genesis 30 is not simply that a husband’s bed became part of a bargain.
It is that people made in God's image were caught in a struggle to obtain from one another what no fallen human being could fully provide.
That struggle has never disappeared.
It lives in modern homes.
In church pews.
In private messages.
In relationships built on fear.
In marriages where affection is withheld as punishment.
In friendships where attention becomes currency.
In hearts that measure their worth by whether someone else chooses them.
And perhaps it is living in yours.
So what do you do when you recognize yourself in this story?
You come into the light.
You stop defending what needs repentance.
You stop pretending your wounds are healed when they are still governing your choices.
You confess jealousy if jealousy has taken root.
You confess manipulation if you have tried to control another person.
You seek forgiveness where you have sinned.
You pursue wise help where you have been harmed.
And you bring your grief honestly before God.
You do not have to disguise your sorrow to pray.
Psalm 62:8 says:
“Pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us.”
Pour it out.
The envy you are ashamed to admit.
The resentment you have rehearsed for years.
The loneliness behind your smile.
The anger at prayers that seem unanswered.
The exhausting need to prove you deserve to be loved.
Bring it all before Him.
Not because every feeling is righteous.
But because the God who calls us to repentance is also the God who welcomes the brokenhearted to seek His mercy.
And if you have never truly trusted Jesus Christ, hear His invitation.
You do not need to clean up your entire life before coming to Him.
But coming to Him means you cannot insist on keeping sin as your master.
Jesus calls us to repentance and faith.
He died for sins.
He rose from the dead.
And salvation is found in Him, not in our efforts to make ourselves worthy.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we secured the approval of everyone who rejected us.
Not after we learned how to perform Christianity perfectly.
Christ died for us while we were sinners.
That is grace.
And grace does not leave us unchanged.
It teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live for God (Titus 2:11–12).
It calls us away from bitterness and toward forgiveness.
Away from comparison and toward gratitude.
Away from manipulation and toward truth.
Away from self-salvation and toward trust in Jesus Christ.
This is why the story of Leah and Rachel matters.
Not because every complicated detail offers a behavior to imitate.
But because the Bible is honest about the people through whom its history unfolds.
It does not hide the dysfunction.
It does not polish the family into something respectable.
It shows us the painful truth.
And then it carries the story forward until the Lion of Judah appears.
From a wounded household to the promised Messiah.
From human rivalry to divine redemption.
From the cry of an unloved woman to the coming of the Savior who loved His people and gave Himself for them.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by guaranteeing that every earthly wound disappears.
But by redeeming sinners, transforming hearts, and bringing a future no human failure can ultimately cancel for those who belong to Christ.
And now I want to ask you something.
Not as someone standing above you.
But as someone inviting you to examine your own heart before God.
Which part of this story exposed something you have been carrying?
Are you exhausted from trying to earn love?
Are you secretly comparing your life with someone else's?
Are you grieving a prayer that has not been answered?
Have you allowed rejection to harden into bitterness?
Or have you spent so long pretending to be strong that you no longer remember the last time you told someone you were hurting?
You do not owe strangers the private details of your life.

And if God has already brought you through a season when you felt unseen, consider sharing a brief testimony. Your words may encourage someone who has begun to believe that their suffering has made them invisible.
Someone reading this may need to know they are not the only one still fighting to trust God.
Someone may need a reminder that repentance is possible.
That forgiveness is real.
That the mercy of Jesus Christ is not exhausted.
And if a particular person came to mind while you were reading, consider sending this article to them privately.
But be thoughtful. Do not publicly expose someone else's marriage struggles, infertility, family conflict, or private grief through a tag.
Love protects dignity even while speaking truth.

There may come a day when comparison returns, when rejection hurts again, or when waiting becomes unbearable, and you need to revisit the truth that God does not measure your worth by someone else's preference.
It may reach a discouraged husband.
A wounded wife.
A young believer battling envy.
A parent praying through grief.
Someone who has not opened a Bible in years.
Or a person who does not yet know Jesus Christ but is beginning to wonder whether grace could possibly be for them.
And if you believe in helping more people encounter biblical truth, I want to invite you into something deeper than reading one article.
At Gospel Warrior, our desire is to keep pointing people to Jesus Christ through Scripture-centered teaching, discipleship, encouragement, repentance, and the hope of the gospel.
We want those resources to continue reaching people who cannot afford to buy Christian books or discipleship materials.
People who are searching for answers.
People returning to faith.
People who need biblical nourishment but have very little financial capacity.
People who may be reading the gospel quietly in places where no one knows they are seeking Jesus.

For some believers, supporting gospel ministry is a meaningful expression of stewardship and generosity, alongside the responsibilities they already have toward their local church, family, and neighbors.
Scripture encourages believers to support faithful ministry. Galatians 6:6 speaks about sharing good things with those who teach the Word, and 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That matters deeply to us.
You do not have to give money to earn His favor.
And your financial circumstances do not determine your spiritual worth.
Not because Christ needs your money to remain Lord.
But because gospel ministry, teaching, resource development, and outreach involve real work, and willing generosity can help that work continue.
Jesus is.
The resources are not our Savior.
Jesus is.
You can still read, learn, pray, share, encourage others, and make use of our free resources.
Your presence is not measured by a payment.
Let them encounter the Word.
Let them ask questions.
Let them wrestle honestly with truth.
Let them discover that Christianity is not about pretending we have never been broken.
It is about the Savior who came to redeem sinners and make all things new.
Before you leave, return with me one final time to that field in Genesis.
A boy had gathered mandrakes.
Two sisters were arguing.
A husband came home.
A bargain was made.
And an ordinary evening became one of the most uncomfortable scenes in the history of that family.
If you had been standing nearby, perhaps all you would have seen was jealousy.
Competition.
Resentment.
A household full of people hurting one another.
You would not have seen the future royal line of Judah.
You would not have seen Bethlehem.
You would not have seen the cross.
You would not have seen the empty tomb.
Yet the Scriptures eventually lead us there.
Not because Leah and Rachel understood what God would do through the generations.
Not because their rivalry was necessary to make Him powerful.
But because God's redemptive purpose is greater than the failures of the people through whom biblical history unfolds.
And that should give every repentant sinner a reason to hope.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have to become your master.
Your rejection may have shaped your fears.
It does not have to define your identity in Christ.
Your jealousy may need confession.
Your relationships may need repair.
Your circumstances may still be painful tomorrow.
But Jesus Christ remains the same Savior.
His grace is still sufficient to receive the repentant.
His truth is still strong enough to confront our sin.
His resurrection is still the foundation of Christian hope.
And His promise of eternal life remains secure for those who trust in Him.
So tonight, if you find yourself lying awake wondering why someone else was chosen, why someone else received what you wanted, or why your life has taken a road you never expected, remember this:
Leah was seen.
Rachel was remembered.
And through the line of Judah, the Savior came.
You may not understand every chapter God has permitted in your life.
But you can bring every chapter to Jesus.
You can stop bargaining for an identity that grace has already given to those who belong to Him.
You can repent of what is sinful without denying what has been painful.
You can mourn what was lost without surrendering your hope.
And you can trust the One who carried our sins to the cross and rose again.
Because the deepest tragedy is not that someone failed to choose you. It is spending your whole life begging for human approval while refusing the Savior who calls you to come to Him.
Come to Christ.
Not with mandrakes.
Not with bargains.
Not with a carefully rehearsed version of yourself.
Come with repentance.
Come with faith.
Come with the truth.
And receive the mercy that only He can give.
